blocks.text: Mills said several agencies were caught unprepared. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said officers dealt with the protest swiftly. Kent Police has not yet commented on the criticism or who organised the demonstration.

Hope Not Hate said the Patriot Platform network arranged the protest. Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas praised it online. Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe also backed the demonstrators, while condemning the use of balaclavas.
The disruption affected travellers, businesses and local residents. Mills said the response should be reviewed, including reports that protesters parked vehicles in nearby Preston.

blocks.text: Dover protest disrupted port

blocks.caption: Protest lasted about four and a half hours
blocks.text: 4.5 hours

items: Hundreds of masked men blocked roads near Dover’s port on Saturday.
The protest ran from 07:00 to about 11:30 BST, causing long tailbacks.
Dover council leader Kevin Mills said police were slow to respond; Kent Police has not commented.

blocks.caption: What happened
blocks.text: Access to the Port of Dover was blocked for hours. Vehicles were also reportedly left in nearby Preston before protesters arrived. No arrests were made, and police described the demonstration as spontaneous.

blocks.caption: Who is being linked to it
blocks.text: Hope Not Hate said the Patriot Platform network organised the protest. Police have not commented on who was behind it. Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas praised the demonstration online.

blocks.caption: The response
blocks.text: Mills said agencies were caught unprepared and called for a review. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds condemned what he called intimidatory behaviour, while saying peaceful protest remains essential.

blocks.text: JLR job cuts expected

blocks.caption: Possible jobs affected, not confirmed

blocks.text:
• JLR has opened a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management staff.
• Ministers will meet JLR and Unite early next week.
• JLR has not confirmed how many jobs may go.

blocks.caption: The company is recovering from a costly cyber attack.
blocks.text: JLR says the changes will simplify its business, improve efficiency and build resilience. A 2025 cyber attack halted manufacturing for several weeks and contributed to a 27% fall in production. Analysts estimate the total cost at £1.9bn.

blocks.caption: What happens next
blocks.text: The government says it will discuss ways to mitigate job losses, but has ruled out a bailout. JLR has not excluded some compulsory redundancies.

blocks.text: On the other side of pain, hope

blocks.caption: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on hope

blocks.text: Femi Koleoso guest-edits the Guardian’s culture section, sharing a personal case for hope shaped by music, family and community.

items: Koleoso grew up in Enfield and began playing drums at church.
He describes hope as the possibility of renewal after pain.
His cultural picks include music, film and a celebration of steelpan.

blocks.caption: Music can carry pain into joy.

blocks.text: Koleoso connects his own journey — from a north London state-school education to life as Ezra Collective’s bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster — with a wider belief in the power of hopeful stories. He finds that transformation in music born from hardship, including Fela Kuti, grime and calypso.

blocks.text: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on hope

blocks.caption: A 75th-anniversary celebration of steelpan
The musician guest-edits the Culture section

items: Koleoso describes hope as belief in renewal after pain.
He connects hardship with the music it inspires, from Fela Kuti to grime and calypso.
Ezra Collective members share cultural picks spanning film, albums and live music.

blocks.caption: Music can turn pain into shared joy

blocks.text: For Koleoso, hope is not an insistence that the world is uncomplicated or that suffering can be wished away. It is the belief that joy may follow mourning, and that people can eventually find solid ground even when they cannot yet see how change will come. He finds that possibility most clearly in music: songs born from grief, poverty or oppression can become sources of movement, connection and celebration.
